didactic

/dih-DAK-tik/ — stress on DAK · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Didactic describes something meant to teach a lesson.

The travel guide is unapologetically didactic, interrupting its lists of sights with lessons on local history.

Example

The science museum's fossil hall was openly didactic: every display paired its specimen with a card spelling out the lesson visitors were meant to take away from it.

didact (teaching/teacher) + -ic (having the character of) = having the character of teaching; meant to teach. The hall's design—each fossil matched to the lesson it should teach—shows it is built to instruct, not just to display. Didactic captures that intentional teaching purpose.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

preachy: Preachy means pushing a moral lesson in a way that annoys - the audience feels talked down to. Didactic is the wider, more neutral label for anything designed to teach; it only turns negative when the teaching gets heavy-handed. Every preachy story is didactic, but a didactic story can still be graceful.

prescriptive: Prescriptive means laying down rules about how things must be done - a prescriptive style guide bans certain words outright. Didactic aims to teach a lesson or message rather than to issue rules. A driver's manual is prescriptive; a fable about greed is didactic.

moralizing: Moralizing means delivering opinions about right and wrong, usually uninvited - a moralizing uncle turns every dinner into a sermon. Didactic is about design: a didactic work is built to instruct. Moralizing describes the preaching itself; didactic describes a purpose, worn lightly or heavily.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

entertaining: meant to amuse and delight, not to instruct

lighthearted: playful and fun, free of heavy lessons

Where it sits · how insistently it preaches its lesson

informative → educational → instructive → didactic

informative vs. didactic: An informative poster simply presents the facts, while a didactic one lectures you about what to think of them.

educational vs. didactic: An educational film teaches you something new, but a didactic film keeps stopping the story to hammer home its moral.

instructive vs. didactic: An instructive example shows you how something works; a didactic one insists on spelling out the lesson twice.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — didact: teach; teaching — from Greek didaskein, 'to teach' (didaktikos, 'apt at teaching') (Greek)

Suffix — -ic: characteristic of; having the nature of (Greek (via Latin -icus))

Put it together: didact- (teach) + -ic (characteristic of) = having the character of teaching. Something didactic sets out to teach you a lesson — often so determined to instruct that it forgets to entertain.

Use the root in a new word: autodidact: Critics kept asking where the painter had trained, and she smiled and told them she was an autodidact.

Word Choice

formal/academic

Reach for didactic when something is clearly designed to teach a lesson or drive home a message—in a book, film, speech, or even a character's role. Be aware: the word often carries a negative edge, suggesting the teaching is heavy-handed or overwrites entertainment.
